newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia to press NATO entry bid despite US move.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia to press NATO entry bid despite US move.

text.p: Slovenia pledged on Thursday to press its bid for quick NATO membership despite a U.S. announcement saying it favoured expansion only for three other ex-communist states.
"Slovenia enjoys the support of at least nine NATO member nations for its candidature," Foreign Minister Zoran Thaler said in a statement issued by the Slovenian news agency STA.
"This support is getting stronger and other members are not opposed to our bid."

It said Slovenia, the most advanced of all former communist states, would pursue its campaign right up until next month's NATO summit in Madrid, where the candidates for enlargement eastward are to be announced.

The U.S. announcement at a NATO meeting in Brussels said President Bill Clinton's administration favoured including only favourites Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic and leaving out longshot prospects Romania and Slovenia.
Slovenia, with a population of only two million has received strong backing from Italy, its western neighbour.
France, a strong supporter of Romania's bid, has also backed Slovenia as have some German officials. But it was not clear to which countries Thaler was referring as backers of Slovenia.

Western commentators say Slovenia meets NATO membership criteria by virtue of its solid democratic institutions, respect for human rights, civilian control over the army and market economic structures.
Its leaders say NATO membership would enable Slovenia to set an example for other countries in the Balkan region.
They also say the country is in a good position to afford integration into NATO and has weapons largely compatible with the Western Alliance.
But Slovenia's largely undeveloped armed forces have little to offer NATO. The country had no navy or air force when it won independence from Yugoslavia in 1991.

Romanian officials also pledged to pursue their bid, saying the U.S. move failed to take account of Washington's interests in eastern Europe and suggested that the Clinton administration could be persuaded to change its mind by the Madrid summit.
